title: Timeouts: what waits, and for how long

blocks.text:
# Week 3, Day 1.1 — TypeScript for configuring the runner

Three small things. Today you edit `playwright.config.ts`, and all three appear in it.

> **Every Run starts fresh.** The studio executes your code in a new process each time, so nothing is left over between runs.

| # | Concept | Where it shows up today |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Objects, and objects inside objects | the config *is* one big object |
| 2 | Numeric separators (`60_000`) | timeouts in milliseconds |
| 3 | `export default` | how the config hands itself to Playwright |

## 1. Objects, and objects inside objects

Named values in curly braces, commas between. A value can be another object — that's
how settings get grouped.

**Expected:** `./tests`, the URL, then the whole object printed across several lines.

`timeout: 30000` has no quotes — it's a number. `"30000"` would be a string, and Playwright
wants a number.

**Challenge:** add an `expect` group holding its own `timeout`, then print just that value.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 2. Numeric separators

`60_000` and `60000` are the *same number*. The underscore is ignored by TypeScript and
exists purely so you can see at a glance that it's sixty thousand, not six thousand.

Every Playwright timeout is in **milliseconds**, so these numbers get big fast.

**Expected:** `true`, then `5000 30000 60000`, then `90000 ms is 90 seconds`.

Misreading `30000` as 3 seconds instead of 30 is a genuinely common mistake when you're
scanning a config quickly. The underscore removes the ambiguity for free.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 3. `export default`

A file can hand exactly one thing to whoever imports it. That's `export default`.

`playwright.config.ts` ends with one, which is how the runner finds your settings:

```ts
export default defineConfig({ ... });
```

You never call it yourself — Playwright imports the file and reads the default export.

**Expected:** the config object, then the string.

Notebook cells can't use `export`, so the real forms are shown as comments. You'll write the
genuine `export default` in Day 3 when you build a shared class.

## Recap

| Concept | Remember |
|---|---|
| Objects | The config is one object; groups are nested objects. |
| `60_000` | Same as `60000`. Milliseconds, always. |
| `export default` | One per file. How the config reaches Playwright. |

**Next:** [Day 1.2 — Timeouts: what waits, and for how long](/learn/w3/d1/p2)

parts.title: Timeouts: what waits, and for how long

blocks.text:
## Two separate deadlines

Playwright ships with two, and they are unrelated:

| What | Default | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| **Action / test timeout** | **30 s** | each `click`, `fill`, `goto`, `waitFor` — and the test as a whole |
| **`expect()` timeout** | **5 s** | a single auto-retrying assertion |

The reasoning behind each: if an element hasn't appeared in 30 seconds, either the app is
broken or the locator is wrong — waiting longer won't help. And if an expected result hasn't
arrived in 5 seconds, something is genuinely wrong rather than slow.

> For comparison, Selenium's implicit wait is commonly set to 60 s. Playwright splits the
> budget in two so an assertion fails fast while a page load still gets room.

# Week 3, Day 1.2 — Timeouts: what waits, and for how long

By the end you'll know why a test can hang for 30 seconds, why an assertion gives up after 5,
and why raising both is usually the wrong fix.

You'll also measure it yourself rather than taking my word for it.

> **Mode: explore.** Write code in the editor and press Run — it drives a real browser and shows you what happened.

## The point everyone misses

**A timeout is a limit, not a wait.** Setting 30 seconds does not make anything take 30
seconds. If the element is there in 40 ms, the line returns in 40 ms.

You only ever spend the budget when something is already going wrong. Which is exactly why
raising it doesn't fix tests — it just makes failures slower to discover.

## Example 1 — the forced wait, and why it's the wrong tool

**Objective:** see `waitForTimeout` spend real time doing nothing.

**Expected:** roughly `3000`–`3100` ms.

That's the whole problem. It waits the full time **even when the page was ready instantly**,
and it still isn't long enough on the one slow day that matters. You pay the cost every run
and keep the flakiness.

Playwright's own waiting is conditional: it polls and continues the moment the condition
holds. `waitForTimeout` is the one wait that can't do that, which is why it belongs in
experiments and never in a committed test.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 2 — a locator that never matches

**Objective:** measure what happens when the thing you asked for isn't there.

**Expected:** about `2000` ms, and an error mentioning `Timeout 2000ms exceeded`.

Two things to take from this. It *did* keep checking for the full 2 seconds — it didn't glance
once and give up. And the message names the deadline, so a real failure tells you whether you
hit a timeout or something else entirely.

**Challenge:** change `2000` to `500` and confirm the wait shortens to match.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 3 — the same generous deadline, on something that exists

**Objective:** prove a timeout is a ceiling, not a duration.

**Expected:** a few hundred milliseconds at most — nowhere near 30,000.

This is the answer to "won't a big timeout slow my suite down?" No. It costs you nothing on
success. It costs you only on failure, and that's precisely when you want the tool to have
tried properly before giving up.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 4 — a failure that isn't about time at all

**Objective:** meet strict mode, so you don't misdiagnose it as a timeout.

**Expected:** it fails in well under 4 seconds, with `strict mode violation` and
`resolved to 2 elements`.

**Playwright refused rather than guessing.** Two matches means your locator is ambiguous, and
picking the first one silently would give you a test that passes today and clicks the wrong
thing after a redesign.

Note it failed *fast*. If you see a slow failure, suspect the element is missing; a quick one
usually means the locator matched too much. The fix here is `.first()` only when you genuinely
mean "any of them", or a narrower locator when you mean one specific tile.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

**When to actually raise them:** the developers have told you the server is slow today and
can't fix it yet. That's a real reason. "The test is flaky" is not — a longer timeout hides
the flake instead of fixing it, and every future failure now takes twice as long to report.

Prefer the narrowest scope that solves it: one assertion, then one test (`test.setTimeout`),
then the whole project. Day 1.3 covers those.
## The same measurements, as a real spec

> ▶ **Run it yourself:** `npx playwright test week3/generated/day1-timeouts.spec.ts`

**Expected:** `5 passed`.

Notice every test **passes** while proving a timeout happened. The transcript this lesson
comes from demonstrated timeouts by letting tests fail — fine when a human is watching, but a
committed suite full of deliberate red teaches you to ignore red. Asserting that the failure
occurs keeps the lesson and the signal.

## Best practices

- **Never commit `waitForTimeout`.** Wait for a condition, not a clock.
- **Leave the defaults alone** unless you have a named, temporary reason.
- **Narrowest scope first** — one assertion beats one test beats the whole project.
- **Read the error before changing a number.** Strict-mode and timeout failures look similar and need opposite fixes.

## Common mistakes

| You see | Usually means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Timeout 30000ms exceeded` | locator matches nothing | check the selector, not the timeout |
| `strict mode violation … 2 elements` | locator matches too much | narrow it |
| Suite got slower after raising a timeout | failures now take longer | put it back; fix the locator |
| `expect` still fails at 5s after raising `timeout` | wrong setting | it lives under `expect: { timeout }` |
| Test passes locally, times out in CI | CI is slower | raise for that project only |

**Next:** [Day 1.3](/learn/w3/d1/p3) — where these settings belong once a suite is real.

# Week 3, Day 1.3 — Timeouts in a real config

Same settings as [Day 1.2](/learn/w3/d1/p2). No new API. What changes is **scope** — choosing the
smallest place a change can live.

## Four scopes, narrowest first

| Scope | How | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| One assertion | `expect(x).toBeVisible({ timeout: 10_000 })` | one known-slow element |
| One test | `test.setTimeout(60_000)` | one long journey |
| One test, roughly | `test.slow()` — triples the timeout | a test you know is heavy |
| Every test | `timeout` in the config | the whole environment is slow |
| One environment | a project-specific override | CI is slower than your laptop |

**Always reach for the narrowest one that works.** A global timeout is the loudest possible
statement — it slows down the reporting of *every* failure in the suite, forever, to
accommodate one slow screen.

## Per-environment, which is the one people forget

CI machines are usually slower than a laptop, and the honest fix is to say so in one place
rather than raise the global default for everyone:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  timeout: process.env.CI ? 90_000 : 30_000,
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,
  use: { trace: "retain-on-failure" },
});
```

This repo's root config already does the `retries` half of that. The pattern is worth
recognising: **one expression, two environments**, instead of a value someone edits before
every push and forgets to put back.

## What a framework does instead of waiting

Most timeout increases are a symptom. The underlying cause is nearly always one of these, and
each has a real fix:

| Symptom | Root cause | Real fix |
|---|---|---|
| Waiting for a spinner to clear | asserting on the wrong thing | assert on the *result*, not the spinner |
| Waiting after a click | racing a navigation | `await expect(page).toHaveURL(...)` |
| Waiting for data to load | the API is slow | mock it, or seed data via API |
| Waiting "just in case" | no condition in mind | delete the wait; find the condition |

That last row is the common one. A `waitForTimeout` with no comment is a note saying *"I did
not know what I was waiting for"* — and it will be copied into the next twenty tests by
someone who assumes it was load-bearing.

## What a reviewer checks

- **No `waitForTimeout` in committed code.** If it's genuinely needed, it carries a comment saying why.
- **No timeout raised without a reason** recorded next to it.
- **Global timeouts unchanged** unless the whole environment is slow.
- **CI differences expressed in config**, not edited by hand before a push.
- Slow tests marked `test.slow()` rather than the project timeout being raised for all.

**Next:** [Day 1.4](/learn/w3/d1/p4) — your turn.

# Week 3, Day 1.4 — Practice

Three problems. No answer key — each tells you how to check yourself.

App: `https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/`, sign in with Leela (`leela@gmail.com` /
`Leela@123`) or use the `login()` helper.

> Stuck past twenty minutes? Back to [Day 1.2](/learn/w3/d1/p2).

## When you're done

**Which of your three timeout overrides would still be there in a year?** The per-assertion
one usually survives, because it documents a genuinely slow element. The global one usually
turns out to be somebody's temporary workaround that nobody dared remove.

**Next:** [Day 2.1](/learn/w3/d2/p1) — sharing one login across several tests.

problems.statement:
**Build.** Measure the two defaults yourself, without trusting the numbers I gave you.

1. Wait for a locator that cannot match, with **no** `timeout` option, and time it
2. Assert `toBeVisible()` on that same missing locator, with no `timeout` option, and time it
3. Print both durations

**Check yourself.** The first lands near 30,000 ms and the second near 5,000 ms. If they're
the same, you passed a `timeout` to one of them by accident.

> **Hint** — this problem takes about 35 seconds to run. That's the lesson: defaults are
> generous because failure should be certain, not quick.

**Build.** Prove that a big timeout costs nothing when things work.

Sign in and open all four dashboard tiles — `Transaction History`, `Pay Bills`, `Add Payee`,
`Manage Payee` — each with a **60-second** deadline on the assertion. Time the whole journey.

**Check yourself.** Total runtime is a few seconds, not four minutes. State the total, and
write one sentence explaining to a sceptical colleague why the 60 s didn't slow it down.

> **Hint** — one tile is ambiguous by text. You met it in Day 1.2 Example 4.

**Build.** A spec where each timeout sits in the narrowest scope that works.

Write three tests against the dashboard:

1. one that needs no override at all
2. one that raises the budget for **itself only**
3. one that raises the budget for **a single assertion only**

Then answer, in a comment at the top of the file: *if this suite moved to a CI machine
roughly half as fast, which single line would you change, and why not the others?*

**Where.** A spec in `week3/generated/`.

**Constraints — these are the exercise:**

- **No `waitForTimeout` anywhere**
- **No change to the root `playwright.config.ts`**
- Every test passes **run on its own**

**Check yourself.** It passes three times in a row. Then deliberately break one locator and
confirm the failure message names the deadline you set for that scope — not some other one.

> **Hint** — the CI question has a specific answer, and it isn't "all three".
